newsitem.title: KENYA: Tanzania urged to treat Rwanda refugees humanely.
newsitem.headline: Tanzania urged to treat Rwanda refugees humanely.

text.p: A Tanzanian policeman has been arrested for allegedly killing a Rwandan refugee and U.N. officials in western Tanzania have urged authorities to ensure that refugees returning home were treated humanely, a U.N. worker said on Thursday.

More Rwandan Hutu refugees flooded back to their homeland from Tanzania on Thursday. Many were badly exhausted after walking for more than a week and complained that Tanzanian troops were forcing them to keep moving.
U.N. officials said a Tanzanian policeman was arrested after allegedly killing a refugee. They said they had also received other reports of brutal treatment of refugees.

A U.N. worker in Ngara, western Tanzania, said U.N. officials there had asked the local Tanzanian army commander to tell soldiers escorting the column of refugees to ease the pressure on them to keep moving towards the border.
With the refugees ordered to keep moving, it had become more difficult to deliver emergency food and water supplies to them, the U.N. worker said.
Twenty-five thousand refugees crossed into Rwanda from Tanzania at Rusumo border point on Christmas Day, U.N. officials said. "It was just another hectic day," one said.
The officials estimated that 415,000 Rwandans had crossed the border since the exodus from crowded refugee camps in western Tanzania began less than two weeks ago.

Some 45 trucks marshalled by aid workers helped to ferry the exhausted Rwandans to the border crossing from a trudging column scattered along 45 km (30 miles) of roads stretching into western Tanzania.
Some of the refugees said they had walked for 60 km (40 miles), carrying bundles of belongings on their heads.
Aid officials said efforts were being made to ferry water supplies to the refugees to counter fears of a cholera outbreak.
Officials at the Rusumo border on Thursday said 300,000 of the repatriated refugees had already reached their home villages in Rwanda. Another 115,000 were still on the road.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR organised a fleet of trucks to carry them 20 km (12 miles) inside Rwanda to ease congestion at the border post.

U.N. officials said they had succeeded in reuniting about half the "lost" children with their families. But hundreds more were still being cared for after becoming separated from their parents on the long trek from the refugee camps.
Twenty children had been born at the roadside.
The refugees fled from Rwanda in 1994 after the slaughter of up to a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Many of the refugees, who included members of the army and armed Hutu militia groups that played a leading role in the genocide, had refused to return home for fear of retribution from the new Rwandan government.

But after Tanzania ordered the Rwandans to go home by the end of December, they began leaving their camps, encouraged by Tanzanian security forces who ordered them to head for the nearby Rwanda border.
